column2: After years of relentless work, Kline goes through such a depression that he cannot touch a brush for months; Edlich commissions from him a portrait of Mahatma Gandhi, whom he revered. Kline paints a gentle, impersonal, detached study, as if he had not given the subject much thought Consequences: Kline returns to his easel

From January 1946, Olson regularly visits Pound, confined for treason after his pro-Fascist broadcasts on Italian radio; he collects and answers his mail and creates a “Committee of Correspondence” to rally support for him. Consequences: The model of the epistolary network Olson will develop at Black Mountain

A fire reduces the studio to ashes, destroying some thirty paintings (half of them painted in the previous nine months); not a book or a canvas is saved. About 30 paintings destroyed Consequences: The start of a series of catastrophes

After the Saturday concert, Jalo has a drink at the Strauses'; he goes out, says he is going home now, takes a few steps on the lawn, and collapses, breathing his last Words: “going home now” Atmosphere: A winter night after a concert, the warmth of friends, a gentle death in music Stakes: The loss of the college's musical pillar

The news of Jalo's death strikes the community; the students dig the grave, choose a stone with Johanna, and Ross sets it in place with the tractor; Brahms's Requiem is sung Words: “Behold all flesh is as the grass” (from the Requiem) Atmosphere: stunned despair, collective mourning through the work of hands Stakes: the community pays its last tribute through manual work

At dawn, a solitary climb to the shop; an anomaly in the building's length; a grimy window, a rusty padlock, a loose board pried off with a branch; entry on all fours; dust and cobwebs; the discovery of the Challenge-Gordon and the jumbled cases; the announcement to Rondy and his blessing received. Atmosphere: Damp mystery, a smell of talc and mildew, Gothic gloom. Stakes: A forced door opens an institutional rebirth: the Black Mountain Press.

Lane's first human image at BMC: a tall, slender woman with brown hair skips ahead of him on the path and stops at the fork with her black cocker spaniel before the big lilac in bloom; with a sweeping gesture she takes the lilac in her arms, loves it, smells it, hugs it; noticing that she is being watched, she laughs and bounds off toward the road, giving him a questioning look Words: She asks Blackie what he thinks of all this nonsense, what all this fuss is about (paraphrase) Atmosphere: Spring, lilacs in bloom, the witness's joyful, slightly embarrassed impulse Stakes: A founding encounter: the woman who charms Lane will be his teacher

A telegram is opened by mistake; the number 47 is seen in it; and 47 people voted the day before at a community meeting for a proposal; rumor concludes there is a Niebyl plot in touch with the outside; the addressee is finally questioned and subjected to a “bizarre inquisition”; the telegram came from a reactionary Republican friend and had nothing to do with the campus. Words: The addressee to Duberman: she was subjected to a “bizarre inquisition”. Atmosphere: Paranoia mixed with absurdity; the biggest surprise being the irrelevance of the outside world. Stakes: Suspicion of a communist plot destroys Niebyl's reputation.

After a failed interview with Albers, Wallen reads his written statement: he cites the accusation of a “bid for power,” recalls the nickname “The Kaiser,” rejects the interpretation by projection, attributes Albers's conduct to fear, denounces his electoral interference as the very tactics he reproached the Bentleyites for, pleads for trust, and concludes by hoping to clear the air. Words: he would like to bring things clearly into the open to put an end to the underground rumblings; must they all be exactly alike in order to cooperate?; he hopes this will clear the atmosphere somewhat. Atmosphere: Serious, tense, almost solemn; plaintive at moments. Stakes: The future of trust within the community and the Wallen/Albers power struggle.

Moved by their two letters, too touching to be answered at once, Albers writes his most intimate reply: growing doubts, criticism of a faculty that governs instead of serving, an attack on the muddle-headed Wallen, a plea for common sense and action, an admission that, approaching 60, he can no longer put off his own work. Words: “Both your letters were too touching to be answered immediately”; “I hate equalization for equalizations sake” Atmosphere: Epistolary intimacy, affection and weariness mingled Stakes: The wish to leave against loyalty

To anchor the distinction between angles, Albers has the whole class stand up; each holds out his pencil at 30, then 45, then 60 degrees, feeling the angle in his body before drawing it Words: Albers insists that the angles be clearly distinguished Atmosphere: A playful, physical discipline, photographed (a 1946 snapshot) Stakes: Making people feel that slight differences produce radical effects

Albers and his students, gathered together, each hold out a pencil at arm's length to measure and compare angles in front of them. Atmosphere: collective concentration, an open-air workshop Stakes: teaching visual perception through gesture
The faculty of the summer Institute lines up for the official photograph; Jean Varda perches in a tree. Atmosphere: summery, festive, a touch of whimsy

Four women, three of them newcomers, work at the same time in the workshop; conversations about pre-Columbian weavings and preindustrial techniques; Zeisler speaks of her work as a sophisticated primitive Words: Zeisler: “I think of my work as sort of sophisticated primitive” Atmosphere: Warm, stimulating, a community of veneration for ancient weaving Stakes: Passing on a heritage: the BMC workshop as the matrix of modern American textiles
During the summer of 1946, Nancy Newhall, who holds no appointment at the college, photographs the Lawrences. Stakes: A hardworking woman artist, officially invisible at BMC.

The young Jouffroy discovers The Armoire of Proteus and understands that painting can evoke an image of the unknown, which leads him to reconsider the foundations of art and poetry. Words: until then, he had believed that only poetry could explore what is inaccessible in man Atmosphere: An aesthetic revelation Stakes: Jouffroy's critical vocation

With little time, the two painters enlarge a small painting of the Last Judgment to about 17 feet square, in calcimine and charcoal, with $5 worth of hardware-store paint; a high heel appears facing the satyr. Words: De Kooning describes the source to Hess as “the four angels at the gates of Paradise,” to Elaine as “Judgment Day” Atmosphere: Fast work, the ink of myth, macabre humor Stakes: Human animality after the war

After years of toil, Kline has been unable to pick up a brush for months; his doctor and patron brings him back to the easel by commissioning a portrait of Mahatma Gandhi, whom he venerates; Kline paints a gentle, detached study. Atmosphere: crushing depression, then empathetic docility Stakes: the painter rescued by patronage

Admitted to an advanced class although he has no BMC degree. At first envious of the others' better skills in technical drawing, he realizes that Albers's courses, Peter Bergmann's excellent physics course, and his building experience more than make up for it; he quickly masters the technique. Consequences: M.Arch. in 1949.

A month after the fire, cancer and a drastic operation; according to Ethel Schwabacher, Gorky, a peasant attached to his health, experienced the operation as a traumatic assault on the integrity of his ego.

The faculty meeting of February 13, 1946, setting up the Wallen-Levi-Rondthaler committee; a five-page report signed by all three; Wallen's statement to the faculty of May 13, 1946. Curiously, in 1968, Wallen no longer remembered the origin of the Community Council: it rang no bell. A five-page report signed by Wallen, Levi, Rondthaler; Community Bulletins of April and June 1946; Newsletter Vol. V, No. 1 (November 1946) Consequences: The Community Council created

Wallen has seen more than 25% of the student body — seventeen students out of sixty — in interviews, mostly simple counseling sessions, but more and more students come to have their TATs (Thematic Apperception Tests), taken at the start of the introductory psychology course, interpreted. 17 students out of 60; TAT tests taken at the start of Introductory Psychology

Design magazine devotes a special issue to Black Mountain (the April 1946 cover attributed here to Alvin Lustig); students and faculty produce a mass of enticing brochures, with sunny images of young students working the land and making art. Design cover, April 1946 Consequences: Utopian “boosterism” continues

Invited to paint a backdrop for Marie Marchowsky's choreography Labyrinth, premiered in April, with little time and 50 dollars, de Kooning enlarges a recent painting on paper — described to Hess as “the four angels at the gates of Paradise” and to Elaine as a “Judgment Day”. With Milton Resnick, he paints a square about 17 feet across with paint bought for 5 dollars at the hardware store. A high-heeled shoe appears near the satyr-like creature. Fee: $50; paint: $5; 5.13 x 5.18 m; calcimine and charcoal on canvas Consequences: The trip to the hardware store is said to have stimulated his taste for house and sign enamels, the material of the black-and-white abstractions
Junior Bazaar magazine devotes an article to Black Mountain College (pp. 130-133). May 1946, pp. 130-33

Guermonprez, the Jalowetzes' daughter, who stayed in the Netherlands during the war, obtains an American visa at Anni Albers's invitation Consequences: She will teach alongside Albers from 1947 to 1948

The Japanese émigré Leo Amino arrives to teach at the 1946 Summer Art Institute; he finds in the rural landscape echoes of the organic forms of his sculptures. The son of an ikebana artist and calligrapher; no space at the college to cast polyester resin Consequences: He goes on carving animal and plant forms in salvaged wood

As soon as the 1946 Summer Art Institute ends, the Alberses leave for a year: a crossing of the United States by car through New York, Boston, Niagara, Detroit, Chicago, Denver, San Francisco, and Los Angeles to New Mexico (late 1946), then Mexico. Albers writes to Perdekamp that their economic limits are made up for by an intellectual freedom they would not trade for a better situation elsewhere. a trip by car, arriving in New Mexico in late 1946 Consequences: a prolonged absence during a difficult year for the college
Shortly after Breton's return from the United States, Jouffroy meets him by chance in a hotel and soon joins the Surrealists. Consequences: Jouffroy enters the Surrealist group

The first trip since the war (gasoline rationing). A stay in Mexico from May 1 to the end of October 1947; visits to Oaxaca, Chiapas, Pátzcuaro, Guadalajara. Josef begins the “Variants” / “Adobes” series. More than a hundred studies in unmixed colors (salmon and pink excepted). Anni buys pre-Columbian and contemporary textiles for the Harriett Engelhardt Memorial Collection. Letters to Ludwig Grote (July 7, 1947) and Will Grohmann (February 22, 1948)

A year's sabbatical from October 1946; Mexico from May 1 to the end of October 1947, the first trip since gasoline rationing. First at the Mangolds' (Lerma 257 no. 2), then they rent no. 4 in the same building. Josef begins the Variants / Adobes (more than 100 studies, colors unmixed except pink, with no underpainting or retouching). Anni collects textiles for the Harriett Engelhardt Memorial Collection, founded after the death in Germany in 1945 of her former student Harriett Engelhardt (Red Cross); the collection exhibited at BMC and used as teaching material. letter to Ludwig Grote of 1947-07-07; letter to Will Grohmann of 1948-02-22
Elaine produces for Mademoiselle an in-depth article on all the ballet companies of the New York season: dancers, choreographers, impresarios, and theaters.

The first Thanksgiving football game in 1946 (or 1947, according to Corkran): an informal satire of college football, a parody program with farcical jersey numbers (Atkinson 3.1416, Schauffler 98.6, Nakata .0005, Fox .606, Sherman 1.000 approx., Roberts 8:45). On the first play, Ike Nakata dives at Faf Foster, who elegantly leapfrogs him — twice; on the third snap Ike stayed on his feet. The players themselves became rough and serious. The Cro-Magnons win 8-0 (Atkinson); Corkran remembers a 6-6 tie with no extra points planned. Dave Corkran blocks Dan Rice flat and throws a pass that Pete Jennerjahn catches with his fingertips ten yards out before falling into the rhododendrons at the edge of the field, on the bank below Lake Eden. parody jersey numbers, rhododendrons, the bank below Lake Eden, a ball juggled on the fingertips Consequences: for Corkran, a demonstration of the continuity between American culture and life at the college; philosophical tensions better resolved on the field

The first play of the Thanksgiving game; at the snap, Ike dives at Faf, who is no longer there — he has leapfrogged him elegantly; second snap, the same thing; on the third, Ike stays on his feet; play resumes soon after, and Faf does not leapfrog again all afternoon Atmosphere: hilarious on the benches, brutal on the field Stakes: friendship and rivalry in a single duel

On a year's sabbatical from Black Mountain College, the Alberses stop over at La Luz, in the New Mexico desert, 90 miles north of El Paso (Texas), in an adobe house they already know, on their way to Mexico. A house of barro (adobe), ninety miles north of El Paso; Josef's letter to Franz Perdekamp: “por fin paz... lejos de la educación y de la administración” Consequences: The birth of the Variants/Adobes series

On their way to Mexico for a sabbatical year from Black Mountain College, the Alberses go back to La Luz, a small desert town in New Mexico 90 miles north of El Paso (Texas), a refuge they had already discovered. An adobe house; blue sky; 90 miles north of El Paso Consequences: Josef throws himself back into painting intensely, far from teaching and administration

At Christmas 1946, Anni Albers visits La Luz, Texas, and the local Mexican churches, the source of La Luz I (1947). a cross woven in silver metallic thread on orange, red, yellow, beige Consequences: the wall hanging La Luz I

The Alberses settle into the adobe house they have already discovered; Josef writes to Perdekamp that at last there is peace, far from education and administration, and they can think of themselves; he goes on his strict painting diet and paints day and night; by September he reports his discoveries about colors that lose their identity Words: Letters to Perdekamp: “en una casa de barro, bajo cielos azules... por fin paz”; “es maravilloso”; pride when the greens turn blue and the neutral grays violet reds Atmosphere: Desert, blue sky, isolation, laboratory ferment Stakes: The metamorphosis of the teacher into a painter of pure color

Josef writes to his friend Perdekamp from the adobe house: at last peace, far from education and administration, they can think of themselves again; he imposes on himself a very strict painting diet. Words: “finally peace ... far from education and administration we are able once more to think of ourselves” Atmosphere: Desert, blue sky, a house of clay, calm regained Stakes: The artist frees himself from the college's burdens to be reborn as a painter

As part of the 1947 reform, Cruz founds this course based on the ideas of De Stijl and partly on the Bauhaus model; the program published in the magazine Plinto (no. 1, October 1947). Consequences: Becomes the Composición Pura in 1949.
Montages dated '47: Monte Albán (17 contact prints) and Teotihuacán (35 contact prints), attesting to a new trip while Albers is still teaching at BMC.

Anni makes her first small work of the type she will call “pictorial weavings,” giving textiles the status of easel paintings — objects of purely aesthetic meaning, without regard to use. South of the Border: ten centimeters high, one of her smallest pieces Consequences: Greater creative freedom
The ten Adobe paintings left in Mexico are entrusted to Inés Amor, whose gallery, founded in 1935, was the most important in Mexico City; a lasting friendship is born between them.
The unexpected black calf somewhat upsets the farm's plans. a jealous Jersey heifer (sey heifer), a black calf

The ravine near the Jalowetzes' cottage is cleared to serve as pasture for the calves; three months of grazing on newly fenced strips of cover crop; potatoes, silage corn, oats, and Ladino clover sown; cabbages and onions above Black Dwarf; lettuce, radishes, cactus, and lilies in the Alberses' garden; beans and sweet corn in front of the farmhouse under construction; the Bennett land (8 acres rented) in spring oats, barley, clover, and lespedeza; 4500 small trees (black locusts, balsam firs, white pine) planted on the eroded slopes; a big unloading fork in the barn; three growing Guernsey heifers; health records and tests. 8 acres rented; 4500 trees; three Guernsey calves
A year after Jalowetz's death, students and teachers led by Eddie perform Brahms's Requiem; Gretel sings the tenor part with several women and very few men. women tenors, few men
A small collection of poems written and printed at the college itself by M. C. Richards; two poems are taken from it (pp. 176-177). a collection printed on the spot

In the spring of 1947, two faculty members resign a week apart: one thinks BMC is too much a college and not enough a community, the other too much a community and not enough a college. Before the end of the summer, both reconsider and ask to withdraw their resignations, which is gladly granted. resignations a week apart Consequences: Proof that college and community are not mutually exclusive

Frank Rice, a new faculty member in 1947, is hired to teach German and supervise the print shop. Having made a career elsewhere in the graphic arts, he is a devout grammarian who teaches everyone to say “printing shop” correctly: “A print shop is where they sell prints. Was richtig ist, ist richtig. Nicht wahr?”

Bolotowsky takes four girls in his jalopy and drives them wildly along winding mountain roads to dreamlike places: ornamental lakes, mica mines, summit lookouts. Each was living through some private torment, but that magical afternoon they cavort and pose while he films nonstop; he himself played along with their mischief. The world seemed peaceful. a jalopy; mica mines; ornamental lakes; film shot continuously; a photo of the four girls around 1947

The local population hates the school for its liberal policy of admitting Black students; Krikorian, in a Model A Ford, is stopped as he leaves town, convicted of speeding and reckless driving, then hit with a suspended vagrancy violation: if he comes back to town, jail without a new trial and the road gang. His battery being dead, the two policemen have to push the car, one of them lecturing him on Southern hospitality. A Model A cruising at 35 mph; a dead battery at departure. Consequences: In effect barred from the town.

A certified public accountant, recruited at 34 to become chief financial officer of the new management team; he understands the real reason only months later, when a faculty member explains the facts of life to him; the treasurer in office is the noblest man he knew there, and replacing him is unthinkable — an unhappy arrival from the start. Consequences: A structural conflict of loyalty.

Five Black students, two of them men and veterans, enroll for the 1947 winter session. No Black teacher could be recruited. 5 Black students, 2 of them men and veterans Consequences: A public statement ending the “experimental” stage of the interracial program

The faculty votes to end the “experimental” stage of its interracial program and publishes a statement: admission will henceforth be open to all students of all races. The official formula: admission open to all students of all races

Only one of the five Black women students returns for the fall 1947 session (she will stay several years); no new recruitment succeeds. 1 student out of 5 returns Consequences: After 1947, almost no Black people on the campus

Lowinsky leaves for Italy on a Guggenheim fellowship and will later join Queens College. He writes to Bobbie Dreier of his pain on learning of the failure to recruit Black students, and of his analysis: if BMC finds none, it is because it does not really want them. A Guggenheim fellowship
Wallen finally resigns; among his main complaints: the pulling in all directions makes BMC an academic chaos. Consequences: The departure of the chief advocate of the “community” pole.

After a wonderful two-week visit, Penn, 24, enters as a regular student in 1947, drawn by his brother Irving's stories about the Bauhaus. Theater is then almost nonexistent there, which does not bother him: he hopes to become a writer while sensing that he will make theater his life. 24; a two-week visit; formerly an actor, stage manager, and technician at the Neighborhood Playhouse in Philadelphia; an extra year in the army directing plays to pay for his studies. Consequences: The beginning of theater at Black Mountain with Penn.

After his brother Irving's stories about the Bauhaus, Arthur Penn learns that former members of the Bauhaus are at Black Mountain; he makes a two-week visit, enjoys it enormously, and decides to enroll as a regular student in 1947. Penn is 24 at the time; a two-week visit. Consequences: The birth of theater at Black Mountain after Wunsch's departure.

Wallen proposes to the Board of Fellows that his chair become “community development” and that students be able to graduate in “community service”: seminars in rural sociology, readings, and fieldwork in neighboring communities (help with harvests, teaching card weaving and drawing, group discussions, lectures and concerts, day nurseries). He offers to contact the neighbors himself. He targets units of fewer than 5,000 inhabitants. “less than five thousand population”; card weaving, drawing, day nurseries, help with harvests Consequences: the Board accepts halfheartedly while keeping the label “psychology”; Wallen reads it as a refusal to get involved

The Board agrees that Wallen should stay and teach exactly what he proposes, while continuing to call it “psychology”. M.C. Richards, favorable, asks harder questions: will the aim affirmed by fifteen students be enough for John? Isn't he leaving the Black Mountain community for the one outside? She admits to a jealousy of those who are going to help at Old Fort. a reaction summed up by Wallen as “do anything you please, John” Consequences: Wallen confirms his resignation

Arriving in 1945, Levi finds the social sciences and humanities relegated behind the arts; he wants to develop them around current and pressing problems of public policy. In the fall of 1947 he teaches Logic and The Individual in Society; Mary Caroline Richards (his wife) poetry and fiction; Rondthaler adds History of the English Language to his Latin; Frank Rice (John Andrew's son) teaches German; Wallen Group Process; Max Dehn, at the students' request, Problems of Philosophy. Consequences: The dominance of art and music partly reduced — a source of conflict when the Alberses return in 1948.

Tasker Howard Jr., a former graduate, seven years at the National Labor Relations Board in Washington, comes back to teach Introductory Economics and Economic Problems of Labor. Natasha Goldowski, a former 100-pound dancer and acrobat turned internationally known physicist of nearly 200 pounds, Russian, a doctor of the Sorbonne, who arrived in the United States in 1942, has published Introduction to the Study of Corrosion and worked on the Manhattan Project in Chicago and on range-finding at Princeton; she teaches physics and chemistry (Hansgirg on permanent leave). Her tiny, ghostly mother, known as “Madame,” gives private lessons in French and Russian.

Molly Gregory decides to resign as secretary of the corporation and to decline reelection to the Board of Fellows; Albers then reproaches her for having sold him out. Albers tells her she had “sold down the river”; Molly judges the remark “silliness”. Consequences: She leaves the community before the crisis breaks into the open.

She leaves her post, exasperated at feeling like the property of Albers and Dreier; Albers reproaches her for having sold him out. Consequences: She leaves the community before the crisis breaks into the open

BMC surveys its former students, notably about their experiences of admission to graduate study; results published in the BMC Bulletin, vol. 6, no. 1, January 1948. A list by name of all graduates 1935-1948 with fields, examiners, and careers, in the Raleigh archives

The print shop, dormant for some time, is revived by the acquisition of a government-surplus press; it is hoped that it will print the college's documents and publish student writing. a government-surplus press; BMC Bulletin Vol. 6 no. 4 (May 1948); the quality and design of official printing improve markedly Consequences: Tite's printing course created
Burlesque skits staged by Penn cause a small shock because they are slightly racy, broad popular comedy. Penn remembers: “faintly bawdy . . . sort of low-class comic”

A push in 1947 to turn BMC into a year-round college, an idea started by Wallen and pressed vigorously by Mary Caroline Richards, for financial and emotional reasons. M.C. Richards: “living year-round rather than skirting a breakdown for nine months and borrowing money to get away from it all the other three”; a five-page manuscript, “Re: Wallen Proposal” Consequences: Hansgirg's revision of the calendar adopted
Besides the informal courses of Penn, Holl, and Tite, small groups study conversational French with the wife of a staff member, shorthand with Rondthaler, and the history of intentional communities.

Kahn is invited to Yale for the first time as a visiting critic in architecture in the fall of 1947; the following year he coordinates the visiting critics and organizes the first collaborative problem. Consequences: He will be responsible for the first collaborative problem in the fall of 1948 (the design of a UNESCO headquarters).

Anni Albers writes that one must take the material in hand and learn from it, approaching it receptively rather than aggressively — a point of view already implicit in her work at the Bauhaus and parallel to Josef's teaching. Consequences: Illustrates the couple's symbiotic intellectual relationship

Albers agrees to become rector on condition that Ted Dreier provide him with administrative support; Dreier takes the post of treasurer. Consequences: Albers will run the college until the reorganization of 1949

Like many of her fellow students, Asawa joins the Alberses in Toluca during their sabbatical year; she volunteers there as an art teacher and becomes a student of the local basket weavers, discovering crocheted wire. Consequences: The birth of the crocheted-wire sculptures
She visits the college to see her close friend, the weaver Trude Guermonprez, who teaches with Anni Albers.

In the fall of 1947 the Moles and Trayer couples arrive (Trayer had been the college's secretary, then registrar in 1942-43); influenced by J. I. Rodale and his magazine Organic Farming and Gardening (founded in 1942), they improve the soil and clear land for pasture, and offer the courses Introduction to Agriculture and Soil and Steel.
Albers, recognizing Johnson's talent, gets him the commission for the cover of the industrial-design magazine Interiors Consequences: Johnson's first professional recognition

Anni Albers writes the essay, dated 1947 and later published in this collection, on design as a coalition of the functional and the aesthetic and on the anonymity of the good designer. essay dated “1947” at the end of the text

During the Black Mountain College vacations, Asawa teaches children to weave palm leaves into baskets and discovers metal wire, which she begins to crochet. she said in 1957: “Crocheting bores me to death. But working with wire is fascinating”; she also studied with the Cuban designer Clara Porset Consequences: The birth of the technique of the looped-wire sculptures
While studying at the Kansas City Art Institute, Rauschenberg works making film sets and props for photographers — objects made to be consumed by the camera's eye.
Enrolls at the Kansas City Art Institute, paid for by the G. I. Bill.

Arriving too early in the morning to call Pat Pearson, he waits for dawn and decides that his new life as an artist deserves a new first name: he chooses Robert, the first name of his German grandfather. his German grandfather's name: Robert Consequences: from then on he will sign Robert Rauschenberg (born Milton)

Follows Pat Pearman to Kansas City; changes his first name from Milton to Bob (then Robert), after spending a whole night in a Savarin café pondering the most common first names. Works nights at various odd jobs, takes classes, and saves to study art in Paris. A whole night in a Savarin café

Olson meets Duncan, then 28; Duncan remembers a conversation about the economic relations between cities and the surrounding landscape, a subject Olson was already pondering. Consequences: The start of a correspondence within the Black Mountain network

At seventeen, already knowing that she wants to be an artist, she visits Black Mountain in her senior year of high school, observes the progressive style of education, and decides to go there to study with Josef Albers, who arrived at the college in 1933, two months after its opening. She had also applied to Bennington and Bard; her father insisted that she go to college Consequences: She enrolls at Black Mountain

The machine-house sold as a package (shell + equipment) fails: no customization possible, buyers already own the furniture and appliances it makes superfluous, curved interior walls unsuited to ordinary furniture, a prohibitive unit cost for lack of real mass production. A package including furniture, appliances, and fixtures; standardized outlines in several sizes in theory only Consequences: The dome finds its real backers in the American military agencies
Cage gives a composition the title “Music for Marcel Duchamp”. Consequences: A sign of Duchamp's importance for him before BMC

In 1947 she makes her first drawings conceived without weaving in mind, exploring the chance of a dropped thread (plate 1), a linearity she will later develop in prints as in weaving. a thrown thread, its random course Consequences: a prelude to the move to printmaking

Frank Rice leaves Charleston for a post teaching German at Black Mountain College, knowing that his father is furious at the decision. The exact cause of the anger remains conjectural: the loss of family support nearby, a slight resentment of George Grice, who had hired Frank, or the reviving of Rice's bitter memories of the college. Consequences: Rice wants to get closer to his New York publishing contacts.

In 1947, twenty-five years after her arrival, Anni writes in English — a language learned from an Irish governess in childhood and grown eloquent at Black Mountain, where she and Josef have by then lived for fourteen years — the account of her arrival: students in “vestal” white, “homemade” bags and dresses, a place of groping, of exuberant confusion, set against an outside world of hopelessness and aimless energies. “Baggy white dresses and saggy white suits”; “vestal white”.

Elaine accompanies her husband to the experimental college run by Josef Albers; she becomes friends there with John Cage and Merce Cunningham and deepens her friendships with Fuller, Kline, Vicente, and Tworkov. Consequences: The birth of a series of biomorphic paintings; lasting friendships with figures of the avant-garde.

During her stay, Elaine paints biomorphic abstractions in oil on brown wrapping paper, showing the influence of Willem de Kooning, Arshile Gorky, Miró, and Hans Arp, but already bearing the stamp of “E de K”. oil on brown wrapping paper; rediscovered and exhibited at the Joan Washburn Gallery (recently, relative to the time of writing) Consequences: Works forgotten, then rediscovered; characteristic of her fierce scrutiny for the next forty years.

At André Breton's instigation, while supervising in Paris the construction of the “Hall of Superstition,” Kiesler makes his first sculpture, an immense Totem of Religions. a totem inspired by a primitive fire-making device: a wooden cross with a rope attached Consequences: the start of a massive output of painting and sculpture over five years

Bolotowsky piles four girls into his jalopy and drives them wildly along the winding roads to dreamlike places — ornamental lakes, mica mines, summits. Despite each one's private torments, they cavort and pose while he films continuously; the world seems peaceful. Atmosphere: magical, carefree, suspended Stakes: a rare escape from Ravin's fears

After being convicted of speeding and given a suspended vagrancy sentence, the battery dies; the same two policemen push the car while one of them lectures on Southern hospitality Atmosphere: grotesque and humiliating, absurdly comic Stakes: the South's racial hostility toward the college

Wallen scribbles in his notes at the time that the situation lacks human satisfactions: people always talk about the college, never time to relax with one another; his relations with most of the teachers seem superficial to him. Words: “Situation here devoid of enough human satisfactions… always talk about college… There is a shallowness and a superficiality in my relations with most faculty here…” Atmosphere: Loneliness within the community, weariness Stakes: An intimate disillusionment that will lead to his proposal and then to his departure

Arriving too early in the morning to telephone Pat Pearson, he waits for daybreak and decides to change his first name: Robert, like his German grandfather, for his new life as an artist Atmosphere: a night ending, an empty station, a founding decision taken alone Stakes: a rebirth of the self as an artist

A conversation about the economic relations of cities to their landscape; Duncan discovers that Olson was already thinking the same thing.
